Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

Negative Appraisals.value: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette:
Imani’s hands, at seventy-four, told the story of a life lived in the soil. For over fifty years, she had worked the same stretch of land, her palms and fingers calloused from the rhythmic work of planting and harvesting. The earth was not just her livelihood; it was her history, a place of peace and predictability. That peace was shattered one evening last autumn, almost a year ago now. She had stayed late to finish staking a row of tomatoes, enjoying the cool air as the sun dipped below the horizon. The fields grew quiet, a deep, resonant silence she had always found comforting. It was in that silence that the man had appeared. The attack was brutal and swift, leaving her on the very ground she had spent her life cultivating, the scent of freshly turned soil filling her nostrils.

In the weeks that followed, Imani felt a profound and unshakable sense of being unclean. She would shower multiple times a day, scrubbing her skin until it was raw, but she could not wash away the feeling of being contaminated. She came to believe that the filth of the attack had seeped into her, a permanent stain on her body. This deep shame meant she could no longer look at her own reflection, seeing only something broken and spoiled. She began to feel that her life, once so rich and grounded, had lost its meaning, a thought that settled in her chest with a terrifying weight.

The world that had once been her sanctuary now felt like a landscape of threats. The rich, loamy smell of the earth, a scent she had associated with life and sustenance, now brought on waves of nausea and the crushing certainty that she was dirty, defiled all over again. This sensory ambush would send her retreating indoors, away from the fields she had always loved. A sudden silence falling over the house, once a signal for quiet contemplation, now felt like a prelude to danger, forcing her to keep a radio or television on at all times, just to fill the space with noise. This constant retreat from the triggers that ambushed her was a desperate attempt to keep the overwhelming feelings of shame and contamination at bay.

Her attempts to manage the horror took on a rigid, frantic quality. When her partner, Joseph, reached for her hand, she would flinch away, the thought of any physical contact unbearable. She had come to see her body as a source of shame, and his touch, however gentle, felt like a violation. This withdrawal, meant to protect her, only deepened her isolation and reinforced the devastating belief that she was now untouchable, forever ruined. She tried to fight the darkness internally, forcing herself to repeat positive mantras—"I am a survivor," "God is good"—but the words felt hollow, a flimsy dam against a flood of despair. When the intrusive memories inevitably broke through, her failure to maintain a positive mindset only served as further proof of her own weakness, intensifying her shame.

This cycle of fear and avoidance began to feed on itself, tightening its grip over the past year. Her deeply held belief that she was contaminated and permanently damaged made her exquisitely sensitive to any reminder of the trauma; she found herself constantly scanning her environment for the smell of soil or the threat of silence, her world shrinking to the four walls of her home. By staying indoors and shunning contact, she created a sterile bubble, which only made any accidental exposure feel more catastrophic. The scent of damp earth after a rain shower, drifting through an open window, could send her into a spiral of panic for hours, confirming her conviction that the outside world was no longer safe for her.

It has now been eleven months. Imani has not set foot in the fields since the first frost. Her relationship with Joseph is strained by a chasm of unspoken pain and physical distance. The belief that her life is no longer worth living has become a persistent, quiet hum beneath the surface of her days. With the anniversary of the attack just weeks away, the dread has become a suffocating presence. It was Joseph who, seeing the light go out of her eyes, finally persuaded her to seek help. She came to the clinic because the thought of enduring that date was more terrifying than the thought of speaking about what happened, hoping, with what little strength she has left, that she might one day be able to stand on the earth and not feel like she is drowning.
